The reproductive biology of the grey warbler (Gerygone igata) has been documented in several field studies across New Zealand, with particular attention to its energetically demanding breeding strategy. Females construct a domed, pear-shaped nest suspended from fine terminal branches, into which they deposit between three and five eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between three and five eggs per clutch], with most clutches containing either three or four eggs. Field surveys indicate that this species typically produces two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], yielding an average of 3.93 eggs per clutch across both breeding attempts. The initial egg volume at the start of development, calculated using the formula for an oblate spheroid from measurements of egg length and breadth, is 1.8452 millilitres , a value consistent with the species’ small body size. Freshly laid eggs weigh 1.49 grams [Ww0 = 1.49 grams] under the thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period in this species, 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], reflecting the substantial investment of yolk and albumen prior to incubation.

Incubation of the eggs proceeds over a period that varies with ambient temperature, but controlled observations show that under an average incubation temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C], hatching occurs after an average of 19.5 days [ab = 19.5 days]. This incubation duration falls within the broader range of 17 to 21 days reported for free-living populations, with the precise value modulated by microclimatic conditions within the nest cavity and the attentiveness of the incubating adult. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge at a wet weight of 1.18 grams [Wwb = 1.18 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the extreme altriciality typical of acanthizid warblers at a temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]. At the thermal conditions characteristic of brooding, 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], this birth mass represents less than twenty percent of the ultimate adult size, placing substantial demands on parental provisioning efforts during the subsequent nestling phase.

The nestling period is characterised by rapid somatic growth, with the young remaining in the nest until they attain flight capability. Under the sustained thermal conditions of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], the time since birth at fledging is 17.2 days [tx = 17.2 days], a value that aligns with the reported nestling phase duration of 15.0 to 18.5 days. This developmental interval is relatively compressed compared to many other passerines of similar body mass, reflecting a strategy that minimises exposure to nest predation. The ultimate wet weight achieved by nestlings just prior to fledging, measured under these same thermal conditions (39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]), averages approximately 6.45 grams, although field records from the studies by Gill indicate that the average maximum mass of 7.8 grams [Wwi = 7.8 grams] is attained at some point during the late nestling stage. This peak mass, with an observed range of 6.7 to 8.9 grams, is subsequently lost as the chick metabolises stored reserves during the energetically demanding transition to flight.

Following fledging, juveniles undergo a period of post-fledging development before reaching reproductive competence. At the standard thermal conditions characteristic of the active season (39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]), the time since birth at puberty is 51.6 days [tp = 51.6 days], marking the attainment of sexual maturity in this species. This relatively early maturation is notable given that many small passerines delay puberty until the following breeding season, yet the grey warbler appears capable of completing gonadal development within approximately seven to eight weeks post-hatching. The time since birth at first brood, representing the initiation of successful reproduction, is deferred until approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth] under an ambient temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], indicating that while sexual maturity is achieved rapidly, actual first breeding is typically postponed until the subsequent breeding season, likely constrained by territorial acquisition and the need for sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation.

Longevity data for the grey warbler indicate a relatively short lifespan compared to many other passerine taxa. The maximum recorded lifespan under field conditions, measured at 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], is approximately 4.9 years [am = approximately 4.9 years], though most individuals likely survive for only one or two breeding seasons given the high rates of nest predation and adult mortality characteristic of small New Zealand forest birds. This maximum longevity is consistent with the life-history strategy of a small-bodied, high-fecundity passerine that invests heavily in early reproduction at the cost of reduced adult survival. Comparative analyses with other members of the Acanthizidae suggest that this lifespan aligns closely with that of closely related congeneric species, reflecting a common evolutionary trajectory shaped by similar ecological pressures, including predation from introduced mammals and competition with other insectivorous birds for limited food resources during the austral summer.
